title: Linear or exponential? Reading growth in tables and graphs
subtitle: Secondary-school level; no logarithms required

learner.topic: Linear and exponential growth: telling them apart from data and graphs
goals: Decide from a table or graph whether growth is linear or exponential
Model a situation with y = m·x + b or y = a·b^x and interpret the parameters
Explain where each model stops being reasonable

intake.capability: Look at a dataset and choose and justify a linear or exponential model

learner.startingKnowledge: Comfortable with arithmetic, percentages and plotting points
learner.background: Synthetic benchmark learner: adult returning to maths

sources.evidenceStandard: Open textbooks (e.g. OpenStax) or official curriculum references

decisions.decision: Offer the diagnostic so known prerequisites can get a quick pass; keep the full core route available.
Lead each full lesson with a visual model and a manipulable activity before the long explanation.
Guided and independent practice in every full lesson plus spaced review.
Size lessons to about 30 minutes and pack the schedule into sessions of that length.

assumptions: Course decision: three 30-minute lessons plus a capstone (about 2 hours with practice), a benchmark-sized course.
Course decision: no knowledge architecture; the knowledge is one short chain (detect, model, bound), so lesson prerequisites suffice.
Simplification: all growth is modelled in discrete equal steps of x; continuous growth (e^x) is not covered.
All datasets in lessons are invented for teaching and are labelled illustrative; formulas and definitions come from the cited OpenStax sections.
Not verified: Common Core standard wording (official corestandards.org returned HTTP 404 to the fetch tool).

outcomes.text: Decide from a table or a graph whether growth is linear or exponential, by testing equal-step differences and ratios.
Build y = m·x + b or y = a·b^x from a description or data, and interpret each parameter in context.
Explain, for a given situation, where a linear or an exponential model stops being reasonable.

modules.title: Detect, model and bound growth
modules.summary: Telling the two patterns apart, writing their equations, and knowing when a model should not be trusted.

glossary.definition: Growth in which the output changes by the same amount for every equal step of the input.
Growth in which the output is multiplied by the same factor for every equal step of the input (same percentage change per step). Written y = a·b^x with a ≠ 0, b > 0 and b ≠ 1.
The amount added from one row of a table to the next when x steps by a constant amount. Constant for linear growth.
The number you multiply by from one row to the next (new value ÷ old value). Constant for exponential growth; it is the base b. A factor of 1.5 means growth of 50% per step.
In y = m·x + b, the change in y for each one-unit increase in x.
The output when x = 0: b in y = m·x + b, and a in y = a·b^x.
The percentage change per step written as a decimal: growth factor minus 1. A factor of 1.05 means a rate of 0.05, or 5%.
Estimating a value inside the range of x values that the data covers.
Estimating a value outside the range of the data; much riskier because the pattern may change.
An upper limit that real growth cannot exceed, such as the space or food available. Logistic models approach it.

routes.title: Core route
routes.description: All three lessons in order, then the capstone. About two hours.

intro:
You are handed a table of numbers, or a graph, and asked: is this linear or exponential, and what will it do next? That question comes up when you compare savings plans, read a news chart about spreading content, or sanity-check a forecast. This course trains one habit: before choosing a model, test what is constant between equal steps, a difference or a ratio.

You need arithmetic, percentages and plotting points. There are three 30-minute lessons (detect, model, know the limits) and a capstone. No logarithms are used.

Each lesson starts from a picture or a graph you can change, asks you to predict before it explains, and ends with a transfer task in a new context. Sources are linked beside the claims they support. Datasets are invented for practice and labelled as such.

diagnostic.intro: Three quick questions. They only suggest a pace; nothing is hidden.

questions.prompt: A table has y = 4, 7, 10, 13 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3. What stays constant?
questions.explanation: Each row adds 3, so the differences are constant: linear.

feedback.2: It is a pattern: the constant difference of 3 makes it linear.
feedback.3: The percentage change shrinks (75%, 43%, 30%), so it is not constant.

questions.prompt: A value grows 10% every year. After one year, by what number is it multiplied?
questions.explanation: Growing by 10% means keeping 100% and adding 10%: 100% + 10% = 110% = 1.10.

feedback.0: 0.10 is the rate, not the factor; multiplying by 0.10 would shrink the value to a tenth.
feedback.3: A factor of 1.0 means no change at all.

questions.prompt: Can a quantity that doubles every day keep doing so for a year?
options: Yes, doubling is a law of nature
Only if the numbers stay small
No; real limits such as space or resources eventually stop it
Yes, if it is measured carefully

feedback.0: Doubling describes a pattern in a given range, not a law of nature.
feedback.1: The size of the numbers does not stop doubling; limits come from resources.
feedback.3: Measurement quality does not remove a physical limit.

questions.explanation: Doubling for 365 days would multiply the start by 2^365; no real system has unlimited resources.

capstone.title: Capstone: advise on a forecast
capstone.task:
A friend shows you two invented datasets and a claim. Plan X (savings in dollars at the end of month 0, 1, 2, 3, 4): 300, 345, 390, 435, 480. Plan Y: 300, 330, 363, 399.3, 439.23. The friend says "Y grows faster, so Y will always beat X, and in 10 years I will be rich."

Write a short advisory note (about 150 to 250 words) that: (1) decides, with numbers, which plan is linear and which exponential; (2) writes an equation for each and says what every parameter means in dollars and months; (3) works out which plan is ahead at month 4 and at month 24 and explains the result; (4) names one limit of each model that the friend should keep in mind. The data are illustrative, not from a real bank.

descriptors: Names a model without checking differences or ratios
Checks one of difference or ratio
Shows constant difference (+45) for X and constant ratio (1.1) for Y
Equations missing or with wrong parameters
Correct equations, parameters only partly interpreted
X(m) = 300 + 45m and Y(m) = 300·1.1^m, with initial value, rate per month and growth factor explained in context
Computes values but does not explain the change in who is ahead
Finds X ahead at month 4 (480 vs 439.23) and Y ahead by month 24, and explains that a growth factor beats a constant addition only eventually
A specific limit tied to the context for each model, such as rate changes, or a decreasing balance going negative for a linear model

capstone.evaluation: You cannot be graded by the app. Compare your note with the model, tick each rubric descriptor honestly, and, if possible, ask a friend or tutor to check that your numbers can be reproduced from your equations.
capstone.model:
X changes by +45 every month (345 − 300 = 45, 390 − 345 = 45, …), so it is linear: X(m) = 300 + 45m, with initial value $300 and slope $45 per month. Y has ratios 330/300 = 1.1, 363/330 = 1.1, 399.3/363 = 1.1, so it is exponential: Y(m) = 300·1.1m: start $300, growth factor 1.1, a 10% rate per month. At month 4, X = 480 and Y = 439.23, so X is ahead, which contradicts "Y always beats X". At month 24, X = 300 + 45·24 = 1,380 and Y = 300·1.124 ≈ 2,954. Y overtakes X later.

Check by computing: at month 7, X = 615 and Y = 300·1.17 ≈ 584.6; at month 8, X = 660 and Y ≈ 643.1; at month 9, X = 705 and Y ≈ 707.4. So Y first passes X at month 9. Limits: a sustained 10% per month is far above what real savings pay, and the rate would not stay fixed, so extrapolating 10 years (120 months) with Y is not credible. The linear plan assumes fixed $45 deposits every month for as long as the saver can keep paying them.
